title: AMA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Memory for Agentic Applications
one_liner: Measure whether an agent can answer questions about long interaction histories by testing on realistic trajectories and by rewarding memory systems that preserve causes, goals, and tool results.
lead: This paper argues that agent memory should not be judged with short conversations alone. Real agents act over long stretches of time: they observe state, call tools, make decisions, and pursue goals that can change. A memory system fails if it stores many fragments but cannot recover what caused an outcome or what objective was active at a key moment. AMA-Bench builds a benchmark around full agent trajectories, and AMA-Agent adds a cause-focused memory structure so that later questions can be answered from what actually happened rather than from loose text overlap.

problem.h2: Why long agent histories are hard to remember
paras: An agent operating over many steps produces a long record of states, actions, observations, and tool outputs. Later questions may ask about causes, missed goals, or dependencies across distant steps.

Many current memory systems retrieve text that looks similar to the question. That can fail because the needed fact may not share many words with the question, even though it is the true cause of the answer.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Benchmark memory on realistic long trajectories, then structure memory around causes and objectives so that retrieval follows what mattered in the interaction.

panels.title: 1. Agent works for a long time
panels.viz_args: State changes, actions, observations, and tool outputs accumulate
panels.caption: Long tasks create many events because the agent keeps interacting with the world.

panels.title: 2. A later question arrives
panels.viz_args: Why did task X fail? What goal was active then?
panels.caption: Useful questions often ask about causes or objectives, not just surface facts.

panels.title: 3. Similar-text retrieval misses the cause
panels.viz_args: Retrieved snippets mention the topic but miss the decisive earlier event
panels.caption: Loose retrieval can fail because wording overlap is not the same as causal relevance.

panels.title: 4. AMA-Agent tracks links
panels.viz_args: Build connections among events, goals, and tool results
panels.caption: The memory structure supports question answering because it stores what led to what.

panels.title: 5. Answers improve at long range
panels.caption: Performance rises because the system can recover the chain of events behind the answer.

steps.text: Use realistic application traces and synthetic long traces so that the benchmark covers both real tasks and arbitrary lengths.
Write questions whose answers depend on events, goals, and causes in the trajectory.
Store events and their links so that later retrieval can follow the interaction logic instead of matching only wording.
Use tools plus the stored structure to gather the pieces needed for the answer.
Measure whether the system answers long-range questions correctly so that memory quality is visible.

paras: The paper changes agent memory from a bag of text fragments into a structure that emphasizes causes, objectives, and tool outcomes.

hidden.name: Causal relevance of past events to the current question
paras: The key hidden quantity is which earlier events actually determine the answer to a later question. That is not always the event with the most similar wording. Often the decisive event is the one that changed the plan, created a blockage, or altered the active objective.

AMA-Bench makes this hidden quantity visible by asking questions that require causal reconstruction. AMA-Agent tries to estimate it by storing links among events and by using tools to follow those links during retrieval.

heat.caption: Darker cells show event types that often matter when answering long-range questions about what happened and why.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is which past event actually matters for the question being asked now.
The benchmark and method focus on recovering causally relevant trajectory elements rather than merely nearby or similar text.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: good memory keeps the chain of reasons, not just the fragments
paras: A long interaction history contains many details that are true but irrelevant. If retrieval only chases wording overlap, it may return records that mention the same objects while missing the event that actually caused the outcome. A cause-aware structure works better because it narrows retrieval toward events that change goals, block progress, or trigger later actions.

The benchmark also matters because a weak benchmark can hide a weak memory system. By using realistic trajectories and long synthetic ones, the paper makes failure visible when a system cannot connect distant steps into one coherent explanation.

math.h2: Rank memory items by causal usefulness
math.words: A compact view is to retrieve the past items that best support the current question by combining direct relevance, causal connection, and objective match, while penalizing items that are only loosely related.
math.equation: score(item, question) = direct_match(item, question) + causal_link(item, question) + goal_match(item, question) - distraction_cost(item)
symbols: overall value of retrieving a past memory item for the current question
how directly the item mentions the entities or events in the question
how strongly the item participates in the chain that produced the answer
whether the item occurred under the objective relevant to the question
penalty for items that are true but not useful for answering this question

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Question: Why did the purchase task fail near the end?
Item A: final error message. Direct match 7, causal link 3, goal match 6, distraction cost 1, total 15.
Item B: earlier tool output showing the card was declined. Direct match 5, causal link 9, goal match 6, distraction cost 1, total 19.
Item C: nearby chat about delivery options. Direct match 4, causal link 1, goal match 3, distraction cost 2, total 6.
The system should retrieve Item B because it explains the failure, even though it appears much earlier and shares fewer words.

math.note: The paper uses a causality-graph memory system and tool-augmented retrieval rather than this exact score, but the score captures the main idea.

charts.title: Similarity-heavy memory
charts.note: Existing systems underperform on the benchmark because similar wording is often not enough to recover the needed event chain.

charts.title: AMA-Agent
charts.note: The paper reports 57.22 percent accuracy and an 11.16 point gain over the strongest baseline because the memory structure preserves causes and objectives more directly.

items.b: Causal links can be built incorrectly.
items.html: If the system connects the wrong events, retrieval can become confidently wrong because later reasoning is built on a false chain.

items.b: Benchmarks can still miss some real-world demands.
items.html: Even a broader benchmark may omit task types, so a system that scores well here may still struggle in domains with different tool patterns or goals.

items.b: Long traces can raise storage cost.
items.html: A detailed memory record may become expensive if every event is preserved, so practical systems still need summarization or pruning that keeps the important links.
The paper is useful because it moves agent memory evaluation toward the questions that matter in real long-running workflows.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small agent workflow for shopping or travel booking. Record every state change, tool call, observation, and action over fifty or more steps. Then write questions that ask about causes, blocked objectives, and the reason a late action was taken.

Compare two memory systems: one that retrieves passages by wording overlap and one that stores event links plus goal information. The demo should show higher answer quality for the structured version because long-range questions depend on causal recovery, not only on nearby text.
demo.closing: The demo must prove that long-horizon agent memory improves because storing causes and active objectives makes the needed evidence easier to recover later.
